extracted.intended_audience: educators, parents, and general readers interested in education and child brain development
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for educational practice focused on the development, preservation, and evaluation of children's mental powers (quality, quantity, tension, variety, control) and on avoiding harmful 'brain-forcing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality is beyond the direct efforts of education; its rarer development, both in nations and individuals, is as yet incalculable: in the early life of the individual it is often latent, and its greatest results belong to years of maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education can overlay, thwart, or expend quality; because quality is largely dependent upon quantity (volume of nerve-force), brain-forcing in early life constantly prevents the ripening of quality. The educator should avoid forcing early production and should wait for the 'mellowness of time' while watching for slow growth of higher qualities or genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity is the volume of nerve-force; unlike quality, quantity may be directly reenforced by wholesome conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote quantity by wholesome conditions — physical education, fresh air, simple nutritious diet, exercise, and by promoting healthy and rapid digestion, assimilation, and excretion. Avoid exhausting production that drains nervous force; provide conditions that build bodily vigor to support mental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension depends upon vascular/nerve factors and the rapid distribution of blood; it is a virtue by which men overcome resistance and are fired with impulse, giving promptness, alertness, and acute sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension can be increased by education and by busying the student with work and a sense of duty; class-tests and modest competitions are to be encouraged insofar as they favor readiness, quick and accurate observation, and modest rivalries, but not so far as to call for 'original compositions', heated and straining effort, or the rapid disgorgement of undigested book-work. Tension is largely independent of physical health and may even exist in neuralgic or dyspeptic persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety or versatility is partly innate and partly acquired, but chiefly innate; it enables men to touch the world at many points and gives breadth and flexibility to the intellect if accompanied by full knowledge of one or more subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim of good education is to insist upon mastery of one or more subjects while also giving a not-inadequate notion of the whole field; avoid excessive versatility that results in aimless dissipation. Encourage culture that is both liberal and profound (general and special) so that a little knowledge is no longer dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control is partly innate but greatly the creature of education; it is perhaps the most precious gift of the individual and the earliest, safest, and most abiding work of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form habits and higher centres by disciplined education: teach justice, temperance, definite industry, social subordination, and sympathy. Test children for presence of conflicting tendencies and set up lines of movement and associations. Do not let children 'run wild' under the pretense of physical development; discipline (body, mind, heart) is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Brain-forcing (educational principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brain-forcing is described as 'terribly mischievous' — it urges genius into precocious fruitage, drains springs of nervous force, excites high tension without volume to fortify it, stints variety, and by enforcing control it breaks the spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true purpose of education is to teach discipline, encourage budding faculties to break freely in natural variety, quicken eye and hand, promote bodily vigor (air, diet, exercise), and watch for slow growth of higher qualities without forcing early production. Modern schemes over-stimulating and unhealthy competition should be avoided; restraint of temptation to early production and patient waiting for maturity are advised.
